title: Sorry everyone, today’s lesson is a bit boring
author: Jo Castelino
summary: Castelino reflects on a teacher who warned a class that the coming lesson would be boring because it had no practicals, and examines why teachers say this. She identifies three reasons: the teacher finds the topic dull, expects students to find it dull, or cannot think of a fun activity for it. For each she offers a knowledge-centred remedy rather than an apology. She develops her own interest by connecting topics such as plants to the wider subject, breaks hard content into chunks that build a bridge to the next idea, and argues planning should start from what students need to know, not from which activities are available. She invokes hinterland, the stories that enrich core knowledge, while warning that poorly planned stories can hinder learning. Her closing point is that pre-announcing boredom gives struggling students permission to disengage.
points: Warning students that a lesson is boring is an excuse that licenses disengagement, especially for students who already struggle to focus.
Teachers can build their own interest in a dull topic by seeing how it connects to the rest of the subject and having students make those links.
Hard-to-attend content should be chunked into manageable pieces, with students secure in each before the next is added.
Planning should start from what students should know and understand rather than from which activities can be done, since students often enjoy practicals mainly for the socialising.
Hinterland stories can focus attention and enrich core knowledge, but badly planned stories can hinder learning.
quotes: I started to think back to times I may have introduced a topic with an apologetic ‘this lesson is boring’.
We might know everything relevant about a topic, teach it to the specification and still find it dull.

So my solution to not inadvertantly revealing my lack of interest to students is to see where a topic fits in with others, how it is relevant in the grand scheme of my subject and encourage my students to make these links too.
Planning should not be focused on what activities we can do but on what we want our students to know and understand.
Any topic can be made to sound dull if it is stripped of its meaning and is simply relayed as a list of facts. Stories can work to focus student attention and can bring the content to life!
But if a student struggles to focus or show an interest anyway, they are less likely to do so if they are told the lesson is not worth engaging with.
